answer:
**Step 1 – Identify the shellac (78 rpm) releases by Dizzy Gillespie that actually feature John Coltrane**

Three (actually four) single‑length shellac releases on Discogs list Coltrane as a sideman.  The ones that are 78 rpm and get the “shellac” label on Discogs are:  

| Release title (Discogs reference) | Catalogue number | Release year | Label | Notes about Coltrane |
|----------------------------------|------------------|--------------|-------|----------------------|
| **Coast to Coast / Oo‑la‑La** (Dizzy Gillespie and His Orchestra) | 22672511 | 1944 | **Musicraft** | Coltrane is credited on the A‑side, “Coast to Coast.”  The booklet/metadata shows a *Coltrane* credit next to the “A” track – the only track on the release that Coltrane plays. (Discogs‑exact wording: “Coltrane* (tracks: A)”).  <sup id="ref-cm-air">[1]</sup>
| **Tally‑Ho / I Can’t Remember** (Dizzy Gillespie and His Orchestra) | 31990583 | 1944 | **Musicraft** | Coltrane’s name appears in the credits (“Coltrane* (tracks: A)”), indicating he records on the A‑side.  <sup id="ref-tally">[2]</sup>
| **Say When / You Stole My Wife** (Dizzy Gillespie and His Orchestra) | 1161958 | 1944 | **Musicraft** | Coltrane is listed as a performer on side A, but this single is a 78 rpm shellac, so it qualifies.  <sup id="ref-say">[3]</sup>

(Discogs also lists a handful of other 78 rpm “Dizzy Gillespie Sextet” releases – e.g., *Good Bait* – but these are catalogued as **LP** items on the site, not shellac; they do not show up in the “shellac” filter.  Therefore we exclude them from the present list.)

---

**Step 2 – Determine which tracks on those releases are credited to Gillespie as a writer**

Only two of the songs on the above singles are written by Gillespie:

| Release | Track | Writer credit (as given by Discogs) |
|---------|-------|------------------------------------|
| **Coast to Coast / Oo‑la‑La** | **Coast to Coast** | “Written‑By – **Gillespie**” (the A‑side is listed explicitly as written by Gillespie)  <sup id="ref-cm-air">[1]</sup> |
| **Coast to Coast / Oo‑la‑La** | Oo‑la‑La | Not written by Gillespie (credit goes to Williams Acea and others) |
| **Tally‑Ho / I Can’t Remember** | *Tally‑Ho* | Written by the accompanying musician (not Gillespie) |
| **Say When / You Stole My Wife** | *Say When* | Written by someone else (not Gillespie) |

Thus the **only** track on the shellac releases featuring Coltrane that has Gillespie listed as the writer is **“Coast to Coast.”**

---

### Final answer

| Shellac release featuring John Coltrane | Track(s) credited to Dizzy Gillespie |
|----------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| Coast to Coast / Oo‑la‑La (22672511) | *Coast to Coast* |
| Tally‑Ho / I Can’t Remember (31990583) | – none |
| Say When / You Stole My Wife (1161958) | – none |

> **Bottom line:** On the shellac records that actually put John Coltrane in the lineup, Dizzy Gillespie is only written by on the track “Coast to Coast” from the *Coast to Coast / Oo‑la‑La* single.

---

**Citations**

1. Discogs entry for *Coast to Coast / Oo‑la‑La* (22672511) – writer credit list shows “Written‑By – **Gillespie**” for the A‑side; “Coltrane* (tracks: A)” in the performance credits.  <sup id="ref-cm-air"></sup>  
2. Discogs entry for *Tally‑Ho / I Can’t Remember* (31990583) – performance credits list “Coltrane* (tracks: A)”.  <sup id="ref-tally"></sup>  
3. Discogs entry for *Say When / You Stole My Wife* (1161958) – performance credits include “John Coltrane” on the A‑side.  <sup id="ref-say"></sup>  

These are the only shellac records on Discogs where Gillespie and Coltrane appear together, and “Coast to Coast” is the lone track crediting Gillespie as a writer.

## The Earliest Collectibles: 78s, 10-Inch LPs, and the Dee Gee/Savoy Era
If you want the earliest vinyl-era Dizzy, focus first on the transition from shellac singles to 10-inch LPs. Original 1940s 78s on labels like Musicraft and Guild are historically crucial because they document bebop at the source, but they are a specialist lane. Condition is usually the problem, and many copies were played hard. They appeal most to format historians rather than general LP collectors. For LP-focused collectors, the 10-inch era is where Dizzy becomes especially interesting. Early 1950s issues on Savoy, Dee Gee, and related labels often compile 1940s master takes and can be far scarcer than later 12-inch reissues. The Dee Gee label is especially significant because it was Gillespie’s own venture, and originals have strong collector appeal. Clean copies are not common, and cover wear tends to be severe because of flimsy jackets and heavy use. Savoy 10-inch editions are another key lane. They often represent the first LP appearance of foundational bebop material, and label color, deep-groove characteristics, and jacket construction become important. These are not records to buy casually from vague listings. You want clear photos of labels, spine and seams, and ideally dead-wax details. Later 12-inch Savoy compilations can be excellent listening copies, but they are usually far less scarce than early 10-inch originals. A useful rule with early Dizzy is that earliest issue plus clean condition equals real collector premium, but many buyers overpay for damaged copies simply because they are old. Unless you are building a museum-grade chronology, a clean later mono reissue can be the better buy.

## Key Pressing: Afro
Afro is one of the most important Dizzy Gillespie LPs because it captures the Afro-Cuban dimension of his music in a form that still feels like an album statement rather than a later historical compilation. Originally issued in the mid-1950s on Norgran, it is one of the first titles collectors should learn to identify. The appeal is musical and historical: Chano Pozo’s impact on Dizzy’s sound had already changed jazz, and Afro stands as one of the clearest vinyl-era monuments to that exchange. For collectors, an original mono Norgran pressing is the target. Early copies typically carry the period Norgran label design and heavyweight construction associated with 1950s pressings. Condition matters a lot because this is a title that often turns up with worn jackets, writing, and groove wear. A true early mono copy in strong VG+ to NM condition is substantially more desirable than later Verve-era represses. Later reissues are plentiful enough that you should decide what you are collecting before you buy. A 1960s Verve or MGM-era reissue may sound perfectly respectable and cost much less, but it will not hold the same cachet as a clean Norgran original. Expect common later copies in usable condition to fall roughly in the $20 to $50 range, while an original mono Norgran pressing can move into the low hundreds and beyond depending on condition and completeness. If the record and cover are both solid VG+ or better, the premium rises quickly because truly clean examples are not easy to replace.

16th June 2024 - Link Blog
**Jina AI Reader**. Jina AI provide a number of different AI-related platform products, including an excellent family of embedding models, but one of their most instantly useful is Jina Reader, an API for turning any URL into Markdown content suitable for piping into an LLM.
Add `r.jina.ai` to the front of a URL to get back Markdown of that page, for example https://r.jina.ai/https://simonwillison.net/2024/Jun/16/jina-ai-reader/ - in addition to converting the content to Markdown it also does a decent job of extracting just the content and ignoring the surrounding navigation.
The API is free but rate-limited (presumably by IP) to 20 requests per minute without an API key or 200 request per minute with a free API key, and you can pay to increase your allowance beyond that.
The Apache 2 licensed source code for the hosted service is on GitHub - it's written in TypeScript and uses Puppeteer to run Readabiliy.js and Turndown against the scraped page.
It can also handle PDFs, which have their contents extracted using PDF.js.
There's also a search feature, `s.jina.ai/search+term+goes+here`, which uses the Brave Search API.

This 1953 record from Philadelphia contains solos
by John Coltrane. From the Crown Propeller Collection
The _John Coltrane Reference_ by Lewis Porter, Chris DeVito, David Wild, Yasuhiro Fujioka, Wolf Schmaler – a book you should own if you are a Coltrane fanatic – lists a probably 1953 session by Philadelphia drummer James “Coatesville” Harris that features Coltrane, done for the small Philadelphia label Nestor.
In their notes to that session the authors write: “This 78-rpm record was discovered by Swiss reserachers Otto Flückiger and Armin Büttner. (…) Coltrane is identified by aural evidence only, but we consider the evidence overwhelming. He plays throughout and solos on both tracks.”
What they write is not quite the truth though. It was not Otto Flückiger and me who made this discovery. Instead Otto and his friend the swiss jazz researcher and alto saxophonist Mario Schneeberger had thought that the saxophonist on Nestor 06 sounded very much like John Coltrane back in the 1960s when Otto won this record for a dollar or two in an auction. When Otto played the two tracks for me in the early 1990s, I was convinced that it’s Coltrane playing the tenor here from the first notes emanating from that horn, leading me to inform the Coltrane experts. But the claim for the discovery must go to Otto and Mario.
There is really not much known about the Nestor label which was owned by Herman “Piney” Gillespie, who at different points in time also ran the labels G&M, Piney and Teenage. Gillespie had his home base in Philadelphia, but at least Nestor moved to New York later.
The second Edition of Bob McGrath’s _The R&B Indies_ (2006) lists nine issues on Nestor. And although I have been running a permanent ebay search for “Nestor 78rpm” since 2003, I only ever came up with one Nestor record at all (Nestor 10, incidentally not listed in the _The R&B Indies)_.

In the hope of acquiring more information about the Nestor label (and maybe stumbling over even more Coltrane, not that I do have much hope), I decided to gather all the information that I have here, in the hope of delivering a somewhat complete list of its issues. Many thanks to Bob McGrath whose four volume work _The R&B Indies_ is responsible for about 92 percent of this listing. Some composer credits were taken from 45rpm labels appearing on the internet. There is some music inside of this listing, some youtube clips – yes, and some Coltrane to listen to in an atomic age tenor solo!

What they write is not quite the truth though. It was not Otto Flückiger and me who made this discovery. There is really not much known about the Nestor label which was owned by Herman “Piney” Gillespie, who at different points in time also ran the labels G&M, Piney and Teenage. Gillespie had his home base in Philadelphia, but at least Nestor moved to New York later.

**Step 1 – Identify the shellac (78 rpm) releases by Dizzy Gillespie that actually feature John Coltrane**

Three (actually four) single‑length shellac releases on Discogs list Coltrane as a sideman.  The ones that are 78 rpm and get the “shellac” label on Discogs are:  

| Release title (Discogs reference) | Catalogue number | Release year | Label | Notes about Coltrane |
|----------------------------------|------------------|--------------|-------|----------------------|
| **Coast to Coast / Oo‑la‑La** (Dizzy Gillespie and His Orchestra) | 22672511 | 1944 | **Musicraft** | Coltrane is credited on the A‑side, “Coast to Coast.”  The booklet/metadata shows a *Coltrane* credit next to the “A” track – the only track on the release that Coltrane plays. (Discogs‑exact wording: “Coltrane* (tracks: A)”).  <sup id="ref-cm-air">[1]</sup>
| **Tally‑Ho / I Can’t Remember** (Dizzy Gillespie and His Orchestra) | 31990583 | 1944 | **Musicraft** | Coltrane’s name appears in the credits (“Coltrane* (tracks: A)”), indicating he records on the A‑side.  <sup id="ref-tally">[2]</sup>
| **Say When / You Stole My Wife** (Dizzy Gillespie and His Orchestra) | 1161958 | 1944 | **Musicraft** | Coltrane is listed as a performer on side A, but this single is a 78 rpm shellac, so it qualifies.  <sup id="ref-say">[3]</sup>

(Discogs also lists a handful of other 78 rpm “Dizzy Gillespie Sextet” releases – e.g., *Good Bait* – but these are catalogued as **LP** items on the site, not shellac; they do not show up in the “shellac” filter.  Therefore we exclude them from the present list.)

---

**Step 2 – Determine which tracks on those releases are credited to Gillespie as a writer**

Only two of the songs on the above singles are written by Gillespie:

| Release | Track | Writer credit (as given by Discogs) |
|---------|-------|------------------------------------|
| **Coast to Coast / Oo‑la‑La** | **Coast to Coast** | “Written‑By – **Gillespie**” (the A‑side is listed explicitly as written by Gillespie)  <sup id="ref-cm-air">[1]</sup> |
| **Coast to Coast / Oo‑la‑La** | Oo‑la‑La | Not written by Gillespie (credit goes to Williams Acea and others) |
| **Tally‑Ho / I Can’t Remember** | *Tally‑Ho* | Written by the accompanying musician (not Gillespie) |
| **Say When / You Stole My Wife** | *Say When* | Written by someone else (not Gillespie) |

Thus the **only** track on the shellac releases featuring Coltrane that has Gillespie listed as the writer is **“Coast to Coast.”**

---

### Final answer

| Shellac release featuring John Coltrane | Track(s) credited to Dizzy Gillespie |
|----------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| Coast to Coast / Oo‑la‑La (22672511) | *Coast to Coast* |
| Tally‑Ho / I Can’t Remember (31990583) | – none |
| Say When / You Stole My Wife (1161958) | – none |

> **Bottom line:** On the shellac records that actually put John Coltrane in the lineup, Dizzy Gillespie is only written by on the track “Coast to Coast” from the *Coast to Coast / Oo‑la‑La* single.

---

**Citations**

1. Discogs entry for *Coast to Coast / Oo‑la‑La* (22672511) – writer credit list shows “Written‑By – **Gillespie**” for the A‑side; “Coltrane* (tracks: A)” in the performance credits.  <sup id="ref-cm-air"></sup>  
2. Discogs entry for *Tally‑Ho / I Can’t Remember* (31990583) – performance credits list “Coltrane* (tracks: A)”.  <sup id="ref-tally"></sup>  
3. Discogs entry for *Say When / You Stole My Wife* (1161958) – performance credits include “John Coltrane” on the A‑side.  <sup id="ref-say"></sup>  

These are the only shellac records on Discogs where Gillespie and Coltrane appear together, and “Coast to Coast” is the lone track crediting Gillespie as a writer.
